chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub from Salih ibn Razin from Ibn Ahyam from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding

A slave belonging to a group of people, permitted for him to trade, a man handed over to him one thousand dirhams and said to him, 'Buy a person from it and emancipate him on my behalf, and perform Hajj on my behalf with the remainder.' Then the owner of the thousand dirhams died. So the slave went and bought his own father and emancipated him on behalf of the deceased, and handed over to him the remainder regarding the Hajj on behalf of the deceased, so he performed Hajj on his behalf. So that reached the masters of his father, and his own master, and the inheritors of the deceased, so they all disputed over the one thousand dirhams. So the masters of the emancipated (father) said, 'You bought your father with our wealth,' and the inheritors said, 'You bought your father with our wealth,' and the masters of the slave said, 'You bought your father with our wealth.'

So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'As for the Hajj, it has passed with what was in it, it will not be returned, and as for the emancipated one, he is returned in slavery to the masters of his father, and whichever of the two groups established the evidence that the slave bought his father from their wealth, his slavery would be for them.'

key_terms.مَأْذُونٌ لَهُ فِي التِّجَارَةِ: Permitted to trade (a slave with financial autonomy)

ai.seo_question: How is the ownership of a slave determined when he uses entrusted funds to buy and free his father?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the Shia juristic principle of tracing property rights through the source of funds in complex transactions involving emancipation and pilgrimage. Imam al-Baqir (AS) distinguishes between the validity of the performed Hajj, which stands regardless of the dispute, and the status of the father's slavery, which is contingent upon which party successfully proves they provided the capital for the purchase. This ruling highlights the importance of evidentiary burden in resolving conflicting claims of ownership among masters, heirs, and the slave's own masters.
